(a) \(a_k=1\) and \(b_k=-1\): both diverge (\(r=1\) geometric, and property (2) with \(c=-1\)), while \(a_k+b_k=0\) gives a series with every partial sum \(0\). (b) \(a_k=b_k=1\): the sum \(\sum2\) diverges. (c) Neither property can be extended: property (3) needs both series to converge, since (a) shows that two divergent series can give a convergent sum, and property (4) is about exactly one divergent series, since (b) and (a) show that with two divergent series the sum can either converge or diverge, so no conclusion is possible.

items.title: Series with nonnegative terms
items.text:
Most series have no formula for \(S_n\). For a series of nonnegative terms we can still decide convergence, because the partial sums can only move in one direction.

Theorem 10.3.13: Series with nonnegative terms

Let \(a_k\ge0\) for all \(k\), with partial sums \(S_n\). Then \(\{S_n\}\) is nondecreasing, and

(a) the series converges if and only if \(\{S_n\}\) is bounded above; in that case its value is \(\sup\{S_n\}\), so \(S_n\le\sum a_k\) for every \(n\);

(b) if \(\{S_n\}\) is not bounded above, then \(S_n\to\infty\).

Proof. \(S_{n+1}-S_n\) is the next term, which is \(\ge0\), so \(\{S_n\}\) is nondecreasing. (a) If \(\{S_n\}\) is bounded above, it converges to \(\sup\{S_n\}\) by the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem A.5). If the series converges, then \(\{S_n\}\) converges and is therefore bounded (Theorem B.2). (b) Let \(K\) be any number. Since \(K\) is not an upper bound, some \(S_N>K\), and then \(S_n\ge S_N>K\) for all \(n\ge N\) because the partial sums are nondecreasing. ◻ ∎

The theorem changes the question from “what is the limit?” to “do the partial sums stay bounded?”, and bounding is often easy. For example, Example 10.2.31 showed that the partial sums of \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\) stay below \(2\), so that series converges (we cannot yet say to what). The value, which is \(\frac{\pi^2}6\), is much harder.

Example 10.3.14: Convergence by bounding the partial sums

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k\,2^k}\) converges, and locate its value.

Solution. All terms are positive. For \(k\ge1\) we have \(k\,2^k\ge2^k\), so \(\dfrac1{k\,2^k}\le\dfrac1{2^k}\), and

\[S_n\le\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{2^k}=1-\frac1{2^n}<1\]

for every \(n\) (a finite geometric sum). So the partial sums are bounded above by \(1\), and the series converges by Theorem 10.3.13. The first three partial sums are \(\frac12,\ \frac58,\ \frac23\), so the value is between \(\frac23\) and \(1\). (It is in fact \(\ln2\approx0.6931\), a fact that comes from the power series of the natural logarithm, a topic of the next chapter.)

items.title: Looking ahead: series with a variable
items.text:
If the ratio of a geometric series involves a variable \(x\), the value of the series is a function of \(x\), defined for those \(x\) where the series converges. This is the first step on the road to power series, the subject of a later chapter, where series of this kind are used to write functions such as \(\ln x\), \(e^x\) and \(\sin x\) as “infinite polynomials”.

Example 10.3.15: A geometric series with a variable

For which real numbers \(x\) does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(\frac{x+1}4\right)^k\) converge, and what is its value?

Solution. For each fixed \(x\) this is a geometric series with \(t=1\) and \(r=\frac{x+1}4\). By Theorem 10.3.3 it converges exactly when \(\left|\frac{x+1}4\right|<1\), that is, \(|x+1|<4\), or \(-5<x<3\), and then

\[\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(\frac{x+1}4\right)^k=\frac1{1-\frac{x+1}4}=\frac4{3-x}.\]

For example, \(x=1\) gives \(r=\frac12\) and the value \(\frac42=2\), the sum of \(1+\frac12+\frac14+\cdots\). At \(x=3\) the ratio is \(1\), and at \(x=-5\) it is \(-1\); the series diverges there, and for every \(x\ge3\) and every \(x\le-5\).

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Geometric series: first term, ratio and value (Examples 10.3.16–10.3.17).

  2. Decimals and applications of geometric series (Examples 10.3.18–10.3.19).

  3. Telescoping series (Examples 10.3.20–10.3.21).

  4. Combining and decomposing series (Examples 10.3.22–10.3.23).

  5. Partial sums and remainders (Examples 10.3.24–10.3.25).

  6. Series with a variable, and positive terms (Examples 10.3.26–10.3.27).

  7. Proofs (Examples 10.3.28–10.3.29).

items.title: Group 1: Geometric series
items.text:
Example 10.3.16: A first term that is not the coefficient

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac5{4^k}\).

Solution. Write \(\dfrac5{4^k}=5\left(\dfrac14\right)^k\). The ratio is \(\frac14\), and since \(|r|<1\) the series converges. The series starts at \(k=1\), so the first term is \(t=\frac54\), not \(5\). The value is \(\dfrac{5/4}{1-1/4}=\dfrac53\). Check: \(S_3=\frac54+\frac5{16}+\frac5{64}=\frac{105}{64}\approx1.64\), which is below \(\frac53\approx1.67\), as it must be for positive terms.

Example 10.3.17: Finding the ratio from the terms

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{3^{k+1}}{(-5)^{k-1}}\).

Solution. The ratio of consecutive terms is constant: \(\dfrac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}=\dfrac{3^{k+2}/(-5)^k}{3^{k+1}/(-5)^{k-1}}=\dfrac3{-5}=-\dfrac35\), so the series is geometric with \(|r|<1\). The first term is the one at \(k=2\): \(t=\dfrac{3^3}{(-5)^1}=-\dfrac{27}5\). The value is \(\dfrac{-27/5}{1+3/5}=-\dfrac{27}8=-3.375\). Check: the partial sums \(-5.4,\ -2.16,\ -4.104,\ \dots\) alternate around the value, as they should when \(r<0\).

items.title: Group 2: Decimals and applications of geometric series
items.text:
Example 10.3.18: A repeating block of three digits

Write \(4.\overline{036}=4.036036036\ldots\) as a fraction.

Solution. The whole-number part is \(4\). The rest, \(0.036036\ldots=0.036+0.000036+\cdots\), is geometric: each term is \(\frac1{1000}\) of the one before (the block has three digits), so \(t=0.036\) and \(r=0.001\). Its value is \(\dfrac{0.036}{1-0.001}=\dfrac{36}{999}=\dfrac4{111}\). So \(4.\overline{036}=4+\dfrac4{111}=\dfrac{448}{111}\). Check: \(448\div111=4.036036\ldots\)

Example 10.3.19: A perpetuity

A fund pays \(\$1000\) at the end of every year forever, and money earns \(4\%\) interest per year. What lump sum today has the same value as all the payments? How much of it is needed to cover the first \(30\) payments?

Solution. A payment made \(k\) years from now is worth \(\dfrac{1000}{1.04^k}\) today. The lump sum is the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\dfrac{1000}{1.04^k}\), geometric with \(t=\dfrac{1000}{1.04}=\dfrac{25000}{26}\) and \(r=\dfrac1{1.04}=\dfrac{25}{26}<1\). Its value is \(\dfrac{25000/26}{1-25/26}=25000\) dollars. The first \(30\) payments are worth the partial sum \(S_{30}=25000\left(1-\left(\frac{25}{26}\right)^{30}\right)\approx17292.03\) (by Theorem 10.3.3, \(S_n=t\frac{1-r^n}{1-r}\) with \(\frac t{1-r}=25000\)). The rest, about \(7708\) dollars, pays for payments \(31, 32,\dots\) and is the remainder \(\frac{tr^{30}}{1-r}=25000\,r^{30}\) of part (c) of the theorem.

items.title: Group 3: Telescoping series
items.text:
Example 10.3.20: A step of three

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac2{k(k+3)}\).

Solution. Since \(\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+3}=\dfrac3{k(k+3)}\), we have \(\dfrac2{k(k+3)}=\dfrac23\left(\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+3}\right)\). With \(b_k=\frac1k\to0\) this is a telescoping series with step \(m=3\), so the value is \(\dfrac23\left(b_1+b_2+b_3-3\cdot0\right)=\dfrac23\left(1+\dfrac12+\dfrac13\right)=\dfrac23\cdot\dfrac{11}6=\dfrac{11}9\). Check with the partial sum: \(S_n=\dfrac23\left(\dfrac{11}6-\dfrac1{n+1}-\dfrac1{n+2}-\dfrac1{n+3}\right)\), and at \(n=1\) this gives \(\frac23\left(\frac{11}6-\frac12-\frac13-\frac14\right)=\frac12\), the first term.

Example 10.3.21: A telescoping series with square roots

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt k+\sqrt{k+1}}\) converge?

Solution. Rationalise the denominator by multiplying by \(\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k\): \(\dfrac1{\sqrt k+\sqrt{k+1}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k}{(k+1)-k}=\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k\). This is \(b_k-b_{k+1}\) with \(b_k=-\sqrt k\), and the partial sum is \(S_n=\sqrt{n+1}-\sqrt1=\sqrt{n+1}-1\), which tends to \(\infty\). So the series diverges, although its terms tend to \(0\) (they behave like \(\frac1{2\sqrt k}\)). The theorem agrees: \(b_k=-\sqrt k\) does not converge.

items.title: Group 4: Combining and decomposing series
items.text:
Example 10.3.22: Properties with given sums

Suppose \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k=5\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty b_k=-2\), and \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=\frac12\). Find (a) \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty(3a_k-4b_k)\); (b) \(\sum_{k=3}^\infty a_k\); (c) decide whether \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty(a_k+2)\) converges.

Solution. (a) Both series converge, so properties (1) and (3) apply: \(\sum(3a_k-4b_k)=3\cdot5-4\cdot(-2)=23\). (b) By property (5), \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k=a_1+a_2+\sum_{k=3}^\infty a_k\), so \(\sum_{k=3}^\infty a_k=5-1-\frac12=\frac72\). (c) The series \(\sum2=2+2+2+\cdots\) is geometric with \(r=1\) and diverges, while \(\sum a_k\) converges, so by property (4) the series \(\sum(a_k+2)\) diverges.

Example 10.3.23: Working backwards from the value

The geometric series \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty3r^k\) has value \(12\). Find \(r\), and then find \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty3r^{2k}\).

Solution. A value is only possible if \(|r|<1\), and then \(\dfrac3{1-r}=12\). So \(1-r=\frac14\) and \(r=\frac34\), which does satisfy \(|r|<1\). The second series is \(\sum3\left(r^2\right)^k\), geometric with ratio \(r^2=\frac9{16}\) and first term \(3\), so its value is \(\dfrac3{1-9/16}=\dfrac{48}7\). Check: \(\frac{48}7\approx6.86\) is smaller than \(12\), which makes sense because \(r^2<r\) makes the terms smaller.

items.title: Group 5: Partial sums and remainders
items.text:
Example 10.3.24: Recovering the series from its partial sums

A series has partial sums \(S_n=\dfrac{3n}{n+2}\). Find its terms and its value.

Solution. By Theorem 10.1.14, \(a_1=S_1=1\) and for \(n\ge2\)

\[a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=\frac{3n}{n+2}-\frac{3(n-1)}{n+1}=\frac{3\left[n(n+1)-(n-1)(n+2)\right]}{(n+1)(n+2)}=\frac6{(n+1)(n+2)}.\]

The formula also gives \(a_1=\frac6{2\cdot3}=1\), so it holds for every \(n\ge1\). The value is \(\lim S_n=\lim\dfrac{3}{1+2/n}=3\). Check: \(a_2=S_2-S_1=\frac32-1=\frac12=\frac6{3\cdot4}\).

Example 10.3.25: A remainder with alternating signs

How many terms of \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty5\left(-\frac45\right)^k\) are needed so that the partial sum is within \(0.001\) of the value?

Solution. Here \(t=5\), \(r=-\frac45\), and the value is \(S=\dfrac5{1+4/5}=\dfrac{25}9\). By Theorem 10.3.3(c), \(S-S_n=\dfrac{5(-4/5)^n}{9/5}=\dfrac{25}9\left(-\dfrac45\right)^n\). Its absolute value is \(\frac{25}9\left(\frac45\right)^n\), and we need this to be less than \(0.001\): \(\left(\frac45\right)^n<0.00036\), so \(n>\dfrac{\ln0.00036}{\ln0.8}\approx35.5\). The smallest integer is \(n=36\). (The sign of the error alternates with \(n\), but only its size matters here.) Check: \(\frac{25}9(0.8)^{35}\approx0.0011\) and \(\frac{25}9(0.8)^{36}\approx0.00088\).

items.title: Group 6: Series with a variable, and positive terms
items.text:
Example 10.3.26: A ratio that is a fraction in \(x\)

For which \(x\) does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(\frac2{x-1}\right)^k\) converge? Find its value there.

Solution. This is geometric with \(t=1\) and \(r=\dfrac2{x-1}\) (\(x\ne1\)). It converges exactly when \(\left|\dfrac2{x-1}\right|<1\), that is \(|x-1|>2\), so \(x<-1\) or \(x>3\). The value is \(\dfrac1{1-\frac2{x-1}}=\dfrac{x-1}{x-3}\). Check: at \(x=5\) the ratio is \(\frac12\) and the value is \(2=\frac{4}{2}\); at \(x=-3\) the ratio is \(-\frac12\) and the value is \(\frac23=\frac{-4}{-6}\).

Example 10.3.27: Positive terms, bounded partial sums

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{2^k+k}\) converges, and find an interval that contains its value.

Solution. The terms are positive, and \(2^k+k>2^k\), so \(\dfrac1{2^k+k}<\dfrac1{2^k}\). Hence \(S_n<\sum_{k=1}^n2^{-k}=1-2^{-n}<1\) for all \(n\): the partial sums are bounded above by \(1\) and the series converges (Theorem 10.3.13). By part (a) of that theorem the value is at least every partial sum; \(S_3=\frac13+\frac16+\frac1{11}=\frac{13}{22}\approx0.59\). So the value lies between \(\frac{13}{22}\) and \(1\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 10.3.28: A series that diverges by the definition

Prove that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty(-1)^{k+1}k=1-2+3-4+\cdots\) diverges.

Plan. Find a formula for the partial sums and show that they are unbounded; a convergent sequence is bounded (Theorem B.2).

Proof. Claim: \(S_{2j-1}=j\) and \(S_{2j}=-j\) for every \(j\ge1\). For \(j=1\): \(S_1=1\) and \(S_2=1-2=-1\). If the claim holds for \(j\), then \(S_{2j+1}=S_{2j}+(2j+1)=-j+2j+1=j+1\) and \(S_{2j+2}=S_{2j+1}-(2j+2)=j+1-2j-2=-(j+1)\), which is the claim for \(j+1\). By induction it holds for all \(j\). Therefore \(|S_n|\ge\frac n2\) for every \(n\), so \(\{S_n\}\) is unbounded, hence divergent. ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to say “the signs alternate, so the series converges”. Alternating signs alone guarantee nothing: here the terms grow, and the partial sums swing ever more widely.

Example 10.3.29: Using the properties of series in a proof

Prove that if \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) converges to \(A\), then \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty(a_k+a_{k+1})\) converges to \(2A-a_1\).

Plan. The series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k+1}\) has the terms \(a_2,a_3,\dots\), which is the tail of \(\sum a_k\). Use property (5) for the tail and property (3) to add.

Proof. By property (5) with \(M=2\), \(\sum_{k=2}^\infty a_k\) converges and equals \(A-a_1\). The series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k+1}\) has the same terms in the same order (\(a_2,a_3,\dots\)), hence the same partial sums, so it converges to \(A-a_1\). By property (3) the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty(a_k+a_{k+1})\) converges to \(A+(A-a_1)=2A-a_1\). ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to answer \(2A\), forgetting that \(\sum a_{k+1}\) is missing the first term \(a_1\). A check: for \(a_k=\left(\frac12\right)^k\) we have \(A=1\), \(a_1=\frac12\), and \(\sum\left(\frac1{2^k}+\frac1{2^{k+1}}\right)=\sum\frac3{2^{k+1}}=\frac32=2\cdot1-\frac12\).

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 10.3.1. (a) \(t=2\), \(r=\frac15\), converges, value \(\frac2{4/5}=\frac52\). (b) The first term is at \(k=3\): \(t=\left(-\frac12\right)^3=-\frac18\), \(r=-\frac12\), converges, value \(\frac{-1/8}{3/2}=-\frac1{12}\). (c) \(\frac{4^k}{3^{k+1}}=\frac13\left(\frac43\right)^k\), so \(r=\frac43>1\) and the series diverges.

Knowledge Check 10.3.2. (a) With \(b_k=\frac1{2k}\to0\) the term is \(b_k-b_{k+1}\), so the value is \(b_1=\frac12\). (b) \(\frac2{k^2-1}=\frac1{k-1}-\frac1{k+1}\); with \(b_k=\frac1{k-1}\to0\) and step \(2\) starting at \(k=2\), the value is \(b_2+b_3=1+\frac12=\frac32\). (c) \(S_n=\sqrt1-\sqrt{n+1}=1-\sqrt{n+1}\to-\infty\), so the series diverges.

Knowledge Check 10.3.3. (a) Both series are geometric with \(|r|<1\): \(\frac2{1-1/3}=3\) and \(\frac5{1-1/10}=\frac{50}9\), so the value is \(3+\frac{50}9=\frac{77}9\). (b) \(\sum\left(\frac9{10}\right)^k\) converges (value \(10\)), while \(\sum2\left(\frac{11}{10}\right)^k\) diverges (\(r=1.1\)), so \(\sum-2\left(\frac{11}{10}\right)^k\) diverges by property (2); by property (4) the combined series diverges. (c) \(t=\frac1{32}\), \(r=\frac12\), value \(\frac{1/32}{1/2}=\frac1{16}\); or \(2-\left(1+\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac1{16}\right)=\frac1{16}\) by property (5).

items.title: 10.4 The Divergence and Integral Tests
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

The terms of \(1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\cdots\) shrink to \(0\), and the sum of the first million of them is only about \(14.4\). Does the series settle down at some number like \(15\), or does it grow without bound? Nothing in the last section can say: there is no formula for \(S_n\), and the terms are positive, so convergence is equivalent to boundedness (Theorem 10.3.13) but we do not yet know whether the partial sums are bounded. This section gives two tools. The first is a one-line test that catches many divergent series. The second compares a series with an improper integral, which settles the harmonic series and every series \(\sum1/k^p\), and also tells us how far a partial sum can be from the full sum.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • apply the Divergence Test, and explain why it can prove divergence but never convergence;

  • prove that the harmonic series diverges, and say how slowly its partial sums grow;

  • apply the Integral Test: check that the function is positive, continuous and decreasing, evaluate the improper integral, and state the conclusion;

  • decide convergence of every \(p\)-series and use \(p\)-series as a yardstick;

  • bound the sum of a convergent series and the error of a partial sum, and find how many terms are enough;

  • prove the main theorems of this section.

items.title: The Divergence Test
items.text:
Theorem 10.4.1: Divergence Test

If \(\sum a_k\) converges, then \(\lim_{k o\infty}a_k=0\). Equivalently, if \(\lim_{k o\infty}a_k\) does not exist or is not \(0\), then \(\sum a_k\) diverges.

Proof. Let \(S_n=a_M+\cdots+a_{M+n-1}\) be the partial sums and suppose \(S_n o S\). Then \(S_{n+1} o S\) as well (Theorem B.3), and the next term is the difference of two consecutive partial sums, \(a_{M+n}=S_{n+1}-S_n\). By the limit laws,

\[a_{M+n}=S_{n+1}-S_n\ \longrightarrow\ S-S=0 .\]

So the sequence \(a_{M+n}\), which is \(\{a_k\}\) with its first \(M\) terms dropped, tends to \(0\), and therefore \(a_k o0\) (Theorem B.3). The second sentence is the contrapositive of the first. ◻ ∎

In words: if the terms do not tend to zero, the partial sums cannot settle down, because each new term moves the sum by a definite amount. Be careful about which way the theorem points. It lets us reject a series; it can never be used to accept one.

Example 10.4.2: Using the Divergence Test

Decide which of these series the Divergence Test shows to diverge, and which it cannot decide. (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{2k^2+1}{k^2+3k}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty(-1)^k rac{k+2}{k}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty k\sin rac1k\); (d) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac1{k^2}\) and \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac1k\).

Solution. In each case look at \(\lim a_k\).

(a) Dividing by \(k^2\), \(a_k=\dfrac{2+1/k^2}{1+3/k} o2 e0\). The series diverges.

(b) \(|a_k|=\dfrac{k+2}k o1\), so the terms are close to \(+1\) for even \(k\) and close to \(-1\) for odd \(k\). Two subsequences have different limits, so \(\lim a_k\) does not exist (Theorem C.2), in particular it is not \(0\). The series diverges.

(c) By the limit of \(f(n)\) (Example 10.2.9), \(k\sin rac1k o1 e0\). The series diverges.

(d) Here \( rac1{k^2} o0\) and \( rac1k o0\). The test says nothing: the terms tend to \(0\) but that does not decide convergence.

Example 10.4.3: Limits from the previous section feed the test

Apply the Divergence Test where it can be applied: (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left(1+ rac2k ight)^k\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{k!}{10^k}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{10^k}{k!}\).

Solution. (a) Take logarithms: \(\ln a_k=k\ln\left(1+ rac2k ight)=\dfrac{\ln(1+2/x)}{1/x}\) at \(x=k\). By l’Hôpital’s Rule, \(\dfrac{ rac{-2/x^2}{1+2/x}}{-1/x^2}=\dfrac2{1+2/x} o2\), so \(\ln a_k o2\), and since the exponential function is continuous (Theorem 10.2.6), \(a_k o e^2\approx7.39 e0\). The series diverges.

(b) By Theorem 10.2.13(c), \( rac{10^k}{k!} o0\) through positive values, so the reciprocal \( rac{k!}{10^k} o\infty\). The terms do not tend to \(0\) and the series diverges. (The terms first exceed \(1\) at \(k=25\): \( rac{25!}{10^{25}}\approx1.55\).)

(c) Now \( rac{10^k}{k!} o0\) by the same theorem. The test is inconclusive. (This series does converge, as a later test will show; the Divergence Test cannot tell.)

Knowledge Check 10.4.1: The Divergence Test

For each series, say whether the Divergence Test shows divergence or is inconclusive, and why: (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{3k+1}{2k+5}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty(-1)^k\); (c) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac1{k+10}\).

items.title: The harmonic series
items.text:
Theorem 10.4.4: The harmonic series

The harmonic series \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1k\) diverges, although its terms tend to \(0\). More precisely, \(H_{2^m}\ge1+\dfrac m2\) for every integer \(m\ge0\), where \(H_n=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n\).

Proof. We show by induction that \(H_{2^m}\ge1+\frac m2\). For \(m=0\): \(H_1=1\). For the inductive step, the terms added between \(H_{2^m}\) and \(H_{2^{m+1}}\) are \(\frac1{2^m+1},\dots,\frac1{2^{m+1}}\), which are \(2^m\) numbers, each at least the smallest of them, \(\frac1{2^{m+1}}\). So

\[H_{2^{m+1}}-H_{2^m}\ge2^m\cdot\frac1{2^{m+1}}=\frac12 ,\]

and the inductive hypothesis gives \(H_{2^{m+1}}\ge1+\frac m2+\frac12=1+\frac{m+1}2\).

The partial sums \(H_n\) are increasing (the terms are positive) and the subsequence \(H_{2^m}\ge1+\frac m2\) is not bounded above, so \(\{H_n\}\) is not bounded above. By Theorem 10.3.13(b), \(H_n\to\infty\). ◻ ∎

Example 10.4.5: How slowly does the harmonic series diverge?

How many terms are needed for the partial sums \(H_n\) to exceed \(10\)?

Solution. The theorem gives \(H_{2^m}\ge1+\frac m2\), which reaches \(10\) when \(m=18\). So \(2^{18}=262144\) terms are enough. That is generous: in fact \(H_n\) first exceeds \(10\) at \(n=12367\) (\(H_{12366}\approx9.99996\) and \(H_{12367}\approx10.00004\)). Even so, adding a million terms gives only \(H_{10^6}\approx14.39\). A series whose partial sums need more than \(10^{4}\) terms to reach \(10\) is a vivid reminder that a table of values cannot decide convergence (compare Pause and think 10.1.2).

The converse of the Divergence Test is false

The harmonic series has \(a_k=\frac1k\to0\), yet it diverges. So “\(a_k\to0\)” is necessary for convergence but not sufficient. Whenever \(a_k\to0\), some other test must decide.

Pause and think 10.4.1: Two series with terms tending to zero

Both \(\sum\frac1k\) and \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\) have terms tending to \(0\). Compare how many terms lie between \(2^m\) and \(2^{m+1}\) and how big each of those terms is for each series. What does this suggest about the rate at which the terms must shrink for a series of positive terms to converge?

Answer and discussion

Between \(2^m\) and \(2^{m+1}\) there are \(2^m\) terms. For \(\sum\frac1k\) each of them is at least \(\frac1{2^{m+1}}\), so the block contributes at least \(\frac12\), and every block does, so the total is infinite. For \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\) each term in the block is at most \(\frac1{4^m}\), so the block contributes at most \(2^m\cdot\frac1{4^m}=\frac1{2^m}\), and these block sums form a convergent geometric series. The rate matters: for a series of positive terms to converge the terms must shrink faster than \(\frac1k\) (the \(p\)-series theorem says exactly that the borderline is \(p=1\)).

items.title: The Integral Test
items.text:
An integral is a limit of sums, and a series is a sum, so it is natural to compare them. The picture below shows \(f(x)=\frac1x\) on \([1,6]\). On the left, rectangles of height \(f(k)\) over \([k,k+1]\) lie above the curve; on the right, rectangles of height \(f(k+1)\) lie below it.

The left rectangles have total area \(f(1)+\cdots+f(5)\), which is at least \(\int_1^6f\); the right ones have total area \(f(2)+\cdots+f(6)\), which is at most \(\int_1^6f\). Squeezing the integral between two sums of the series is exactly what the proof does. For a function that is decreasing, each rectangle comparison goes the same way, so we need that hypothesis.

A function \(f\) is decreasing on an interval if \(f(x)>f(y)\) whenever \(x<y\) in the interval.

Theorem 10.4.6: Integral Test

Let \(N\) be a positive integer. Let \(f\) be continuous, positive and decreasing on \([N,\infty)\), and let \(a_k=f(k)\) for \(k=N,N+1,\dots\) Then:

(a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=N}^\infty a_k\) and \(\displaystyle\int_N^\infty f(x)\,dx\) either both converge or both diverge.

(b) If they converge, with \(S=\sum_{k=N}^\infty a_k\) and \(I=\int_N^\infty f(x)\,dx\), then \(I<S<a_N+I\). In particular \(S\ne I\).

(c) For every \(n\ge N\) the partial sum \(s_n=\sum_{k=N}^na_k\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\int_N^{n+1}f(x)\,dx<s_n\), and for every \(n\ge N+1\) also \(s_n<a_N+\displaystyle\int_N^nf(x)\,dx\). (These hold whether or not the series converges.)

Proof. Write \(F(b)=\int_N^bf(x)\,dx\) and \(s_n=\sum_{k=N}^na_k\).

Step 1: one rectangle at a time. For every \(k\ge N\),

\[a_{k+1}<\int_k^{k+1}f(x)\,dx<a_k .\]

Indeed, \(f(k+1)\le f(x)\le f(k)\) for \(k\le x\le k+1\). The functions \(f(x)-f(k+1)\) and \(f(k)-f(x)\) are continuous, are \(\ge0\) on \([k,k+1]\), and are positive at the midpoint \(x=k+\frac12\) (because \(f\) is decreasing). A continuous nonnegative function that is positive at some point has a positive integral, so both inequalities are strict (the interval has length \(1\)).

Step 2: add up. Adding the inequalities of Step 1 for \(k=N,\dots,n\) gives

\[s_{n+1}-a_N<F(n+1)<s_n\qquad(n\ge N).\tag{$*$}\]

The right inequality is the first claim of (c); replacing \(n\) by \(n-1\) in the left one gives \(s_n<a_N+F(n)\) for \(n\ge N+1\), the second claim.

Step 3: part (a). Suppose \(\sum a_k\) converges to \(S\). The terms are positive, so \(s_n\le S\) for every \(n\) (Theorem 10.3.13(a)), and by \((*)\), \(F(n+1)<S\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The function \(F\) is nondecreasing, so by Theorem C.4(b) it is bounded above, and by part (a) of that theorem the improper integral converges. Conversely, suppose \(\int_N^\infty f\) converges to \(I\). Theorem C.4(a) gives \(F(b)\le I\) for all \(b\), so by \((*)\), \(s_{n+1}<a_N+F(n+1)\le a_N+I\): the partial sums of the positive series are bounded above, so the series converges by Theorem 10.3.13. Each of the two statements implies the other, so if one diverges, so does the other.

Step 4: part (b). Now let both converge. For \(k\ge N\) put \(p_k=a_k-\int_k^{k+1}f\) and \(q_k=\int_k^{k+1}f-a_{k+1}\); both are positive by Step 1. Adding up,

\[\sum_{k=N}^np_k=s_n-F(n+1),\qquad\sum_{k=N}^nq_k=a_N+F(n+1)-s_{n+1}.\]

As \(n\to\infty\), \(s_n\to S\) and \(F(n+1)\to I\) (Theorem B.6(b)), so the two sums on the left converge to \(S-I\) and \(a_N+I-S\) by the limit laws. Each is the value of a series of positive terms, hence at least its first term (Theorem 10.3.13(a)): \(S-I\ge p_N>0\) and \(a_N+I-S\ge q_N>0\). This is (b). ◻ ∎

If \(f\) is only nonincreasing, the same proof works with \(\le\) in Step 1, and (a) still holds; the inequalities in (b) and (c) then become non-strict. Note what the theorem does not say: the value of the integral is not the value of the series.

Procedure 10.4.7: Using the Integral Test

  1. Write \(a_k=f(k)\) for a function \(f\) defined on \([N,\infty)\).

  2. Check that \(f\) is continuous, positive and decreasing on \([N,\infty)\) (usually by showing \(f'(x)<0\) there). Choose \(N\) so that this holds.

  3. Compute \(\int_N^\infty f(x)\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_N^bf(x)\,dx\).

  4. Conclude: the series converges if and only if the integral converges. If it converges, the sum lies between \(I\) and \(a_N+I\).

Example 10.4.8: Convergence with bounds on the sum

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty ke^{-k^2}\) converges and trap its sum between two numbers.

Solution. Let \(f(x)=xe^{-x^2}\). It is continuous and positive. Its derivative is \(f'(x)=(1-2x^2)e^{-x^2}\), which is negative for \(x\ge1\), so \(f\) is decreasing on \([1,\infty)\) and \(N=1\) works. The integral is

\[\int_1^\infty xe^{-x^2}\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\frac12e^{-x^2}\right]_1^b=\frac1{2e}\approx0.184 .\]

It converges, so the series converges, by the Integral Test. By part (b), \(\dfrac1{2e}<S<a_1+\dfrac1{2e}=\dfrac3{2e}\), that is, \(0.184<S<0.552\). (The sum is in fact about \(0.405\).)

Example 10.4.9: Logarithms in the denominator

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k\ln k}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k(\ln k)^2}\) converge.

Solution. Both functions are positive and continuous on \([2,\infty)\), and both are decreasing there because their denominators (\(x\ln x\) and \(x(\ln x)^2\)) are positive and increasing. Use \(N=2\).

(a) Since \(\frac d{dx}\ln(\ln x)=\frac1{x\ln x}\), \(\displaystyle\int_2^b\frac{dx}{x\ln x}=\ln(\ln b)-\ln(\ln2)\to\infty\) as \(b\to\infty\). The integral diverges, so the series diverges (extremely slowly).

(b) Since \(\frac d{dx}\left(-\frac1{\ln x}\right)=\frac1{x(\ln x)^2}\), \(\displaystyle\int_2^b\frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^2}=\frac1{\ln2}-\frac1{\ln b}\to\frac1{\ln2}\approx1.443\). The integral converges, so the series converges, with \(1.443<S<\frac1{2(\ln2)^2}+1.443\).

Example 10.4.10: A function that decreases only eventually

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^2e^{-k}\) converges.

Solution. Let \(f(x)=x^2e^{-x}\). Then \(f'(x)=x(2-x)e^{-x}\), which is positive on \((0,2)\) and negative for \(x>2\). So \(f\) is not decreasing on \([1,\infty)\): indeed \(a_1=e^{-1}\approx0.368<a_2=4e^{-2}\approx0.541\). But \(f\) is decreasing on \([2,\infty)\), so the Integral Test applies with \(N=2\):

\[\int_2^\infty x^2e^{-x}\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\Big[-(x^2+2x+2)e^{-x}\Big]_2^b=10e^{-2}\approx1.35 .\]

So \(\sum_{k=2}^\infty k^2e^{-k}\) converges. Adding the single term \(a_1\) does not change convergence (Theorem 10.3.11(5)), so \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^2e^{-k}\) converges too. The moral: the test needs “decreasing” only from some point on, and removing finitely many terms is harmless.

Knowledge Check 10.4.2: The Integral Test

Use the Integral Test to decide: (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{3k+2}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{2k}{(k^2+1)^2}\). For each, state the function, check the three hypotheses, and give the value of the improper integral.

Pause and think 10.4.2: Why “decreasing”?

Let \(f(x)=\sin^2(\pi x)\). Find \(a_k=f(k)\) and decide whether \(\sum a_k\) converges. Then decide whether \(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx\) converges (use \(\sin^2u=\frac{1-\cos2u}2\)). Which hypothesis of the Integral Test fails, and where does the proof use it?

Answer and discussion

\(a_k=\sin^2(\pi k)=0\) for every integer \(k\), so \(\sum a_k=0+0+\cdots=0\) converges. But \(\int_1^b\sin^2(\pi x)\,dx=\frac{b-1}2-\frac{\sin(2\pi b)}{4\pi}\to\infty\) (each unit interval contributes \(\frac12\)), so the integral diverges. The function is continuous and nonnegative (it is \(0\) at the integers, so “positive” fails there too) but it is not decreasing: it oscillates. Step 1 of the proof needs \(f(k+1)\le f(x)\le f(k)\) on each interval; here the integral over \([k,k+1]\) is \(\frac12\) although \(f(k)=f(k+1)=0\).

items.title: \(p\)-series
items.text:
Theorem 10.4.11: Convergence of the \(p\)-series

The \(p\)-series \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^p}\) converges if \(p>1\) and diverges if \(p\le1\). If \(p>1\) its sum \(S\) satisfies \(\dfrac1{p-1}<S<\dfrac p{p-1}\).

Proof. Case \(p\le0\). Then \(\frac1{k^p}=k^{-p}\ge1\) for all \(k\), so the terms do not tend to \(0\) and the series diverges by the Divergence Test.

Case \(p>0\). The function \(f(x)=x^{-p}\) is continuous and positive on \([1,\infty)\), and \(f'(x)=-px^{-p-1}<0\), so it is decreasing. For \(b>1\),

\[\int_1^bx^{-p}\,dx=\begin{cases}\ln b & p=1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{b^{1-p}-1}{1-p} & p\ne1.\end{cases}\]

If \(p=1\), \(\ln b\to\infty\). If \(0<p<1\), \(1-p>0\) and \(b^{1-p}\to\infty\), so the integral diverges. If \(p>1\), \(b^{1-p}\to0\) and the integral converges to \(\frac1{p-1}\). By the Integral Test (part (a)) the series diverges for \(0<p\le1\) and converges for \(p>1\). In the convergent case part (b) of the Integral Test with \(a_1=1\) gives \(\frac1{p-1}<S<1+\frac1{p-1}=\frac p{p-1}\). ◻ ∎

For \(p=1\) the theorem contains the harmonic series again, now as a one-line consequence of the Integral Test. The \(p\)-series and the geometric series are the two yardsticks of this chapter: later sections compare other series with them. For example, \(p=2\) gives \(1<\sum\frac1{k^2}<2\), in agreement with the bound found in Example 10.2.31.

Example 10.4.12: Recognising \(p\)-series

Decide whether each series converges. (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^{1.01}}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt[3]{k^2}}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac4{k^3}\); (d) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=3}^\infty\frac1{k\sqrt k}\).

Solution. (a) \(p=1.01>1\), so it converges. By the theorem its sum is between \(\frac1{0.01}=100\) and \(101\): a convergent series with a huge sum.

(b) \(\frac1{\sqrt[3]{k^2}}=k^{-2/3}\), so \(p=\frac23\le1\): it diverges.

(c) \(\sum\frac1{k^3}\) converges (\(p=3\)), so by property (1) of Theorem 10.3.11 the series \(\sum\frac4{k^3}\) converges, with \(4\cdot\frac12<S<4\cdot\frac32\).

(d) \(\frac1{k\sqrt k}=k^{-3/2}\), so \(p=\frac32>1\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^{-3/2}\) converges. The series in (d) starts at \(k=3\); by property (5) removing the first two terms does not affect convergence, so it converges as well.

Knowledge Check 10.4.3: \(p\)-series and bounds

(a) For which \(p\) does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac5{k^{p}}\) converge? (b) Show that the sum of \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^3}\) lies between \(\frac12\) and \(\frac32\). (c) Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt{k^3}}\) converge?

items.title: Estimating a series: remainders and bounds
items.text:
When a series converges we often want a number. The sum \(S\) is the limit of the partial sums \(s_n\), and the remainder \(R_n=S-s_n=\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty a_k\) is the error of \(s_n\) (Theorem 10.3.11(5)). The Integral Test also controls \(R_n\).

Theorem 10.4.13: Estimating a series with positive terms

Let \(f\) be continuous, positive and decreasing on \([N,\infty)\), let \(a_k=f(k)\), and suppose \(S=\sum_{k=N}^\infty a_k\) converges. Let \(s_n=\sum_{k=N}^na_k\) and \(R_n=S-s_n\). Then for every \(n\ge N\),

\[\int_{n+1}^\infty f(x)\,dx<R_n<\int_n^\infty f(x)\,dx,\]

and therefore the sum is trapped between

\[L_n=s_n+\int_{n+1}^\infty f(x)\,dx\ <\ S\ <\ s_n+\int_n^\infty f(x)\,dx=U_n .\]

Moreover \(U_n-L_n=\displaystyle\int_n^{n+1}f(x)\,dx<a_n\), so the midpoint \(\frac12(L_n+U_n)\) differs from \(S\) by less than \(\frac12\displaystyle\int_n^{n+1}f(x)\,dx\).

Proof. The series \(\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty a_k\) converges (to \(R_n\), by Theorem 10.3.11(5)), and \(f\) is positive, continuous and decreasing on \([n+1,\infty)\), so the Integral Test with \(N\) replaced by \(n+1\) applies: the integral \(\int_{n+1}^\infty f\) converges, and part (b) gives

\[\int_{n+1}^\infty f(x)\,dx<R_n<a_{n+1}+\int_{n+1}^\infty f(x)\,dx .\]

This is the lower bound. For the upper bound, Step 1 of the proof of the Integral Test gives \(a_{n+1}<\int_n^{n+1}f\), so \(R_n<\int_n^{n+1}f+\int_{n+1}^\infty f=\int_n^\infty f\). Adding \(s_n\) to each side gives the bounds \(L_n<S<U_n\). Finally \(U_n-L_n=\int_n^\infty f-\int_{n+1}^\infty f=\int_n^{n+1}f<a_n\) by Step 1, and the midpoint of an interval of length \(U_n-L_n\) that contains \(S\) is within half that length of \(S\). ◻ ∎

Example 10.4.14: How many terms are enough?

How many terms of \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^3}\) guarantee an error less than \(0.001\)?

Solution. With \(f(x)=x^{-3}\), \(\displaystyle\int_n^\infty x^{-3}\,dx=\frac1{2n^2}\). The theorem gives \(\dfrac1{2(n+1)^2}<R_n<\dfrac1{2n^2}\). For a guarantee use the upper bound: \(\frac1{2n^2}<0.001\) when \(n^2>500\), that is \(n\ge23\) (since \(22^2=484<500<529=23^2\)). So \(23\) terms suffice. Can fewer do? The lower bound says \(R_{21}>\frac1{2\cdot22^2}\approx0.00103>0.001\), so \(21\) terms do not. For \(n=22\) the bounds \(0.000945<R_{22}<0.001033\) straddle \(0.001\) and cannot decide; the true remainder is \(R_{22}\approx0.000987\), so \(22\) terms happen to be enough.

Example 10.4.15: Estimating \(\sum1/k^2\) from ten terms

Use \(n=10\) to bracket \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2}\) and estimate it by the midpoint.

Solution. The partial sum is \(s_{10}=\sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac1{k^2}\approx1.549768\). With \(f(x)=x^{-2}\), \(\int_{11}^\infty f=\frac1{11}\) and \(\int_{10}^\infty f=\frac1{10}\), so

\[1.640677\approx L_{10}=s_{10}+\frac1{11}<S<s_{10}+\frac1{10}=U_{10}\approx1.649768 .\]

The midpoint is \(\approx1.645222\), and the error is less than \(\frac12(U_{10}-L_{10})=\frac12\cdot\frac1{110}=\frac1{220}\approx0.0045\). (The exact sum is \(\frac{\pi^2}6\approx1.644934\), so the actual error is about \(0.0003\).)

Pause and think 10.4.3: The integral is not the sum

The series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{2^k}\) has sum \(1\). Compute \(\int_1^\infty2^{-x}\,dx\), check the inequality \(I<S<a_1+I\), and explain why the integral can never equal the sum of the series.

Answer and discussion

\(\int_1^\infty2^{-x}\,dx=\left[-\frac{2^{-x}}{\ln2}\right]_1^\infty=\frac1{2\ln2}\approx0.721\). Then \(0.721<S=1<a_1+I=\frac12+0.721=1.221\), so the inequality holds. The integral is always strictly less than the sum because each rectangle of height \(a_k\) over \([k,k+1]\) sticks out strictly above the curve (Step 1 of the proof): the sum is the total area of rectangles above the curve, the integral is the area under it, and the difference \(\sum p_k\) is a positive number. Also the sum is strictly less than \(a_N+I\) because the rectangles on the right lie strictly below it.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. The Divergence Test (Examples 10.4.16–10.4.17).

  2. The Integral Test (Examples 10.4.18–10.4.19).

  3. \(p\)-series and combinations (Examples 10.4.20–10.4.21).

  4. Hypotheses and the starting index (Examples 10.4.22–10.4.23).

  5. Estimates and remainders (Examples 10.4.24–10.4.25).

  6. Applications: harmonic bounds and slow convergence (Examples 10.4.26–10.4.27).

  7. Proofs (Examples 10.4.28–10.4.29).

items.title: Group 1: The Divergence Test
items.text:
Example 10.4.16: A rational term

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{5k^2-2}{3k^2+k}\) converge?

Solution. Divide numerator and denominator by \(k^2\): \(a_k=\dfrac{5-2/k^2}{3+1/k}\to\dfrac53\ne0\). By the Divergence Test the series diverges. Check: \(a_{1000}=\dfrac{4999998}{3001000}\approx1.666\), already close to \(\frac53\), far from \(0\).

Example 10.4.17: A term that tends to \(e^{-1}\)

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left(\frac k{k+1}\right)^k\) converge?

Solution. Take logarithms: \(\ln a_k=k\ln\dfrac k{k+1}=-k\ln\left(1+\dfrac1k\right)=-\dfrac{\ln(1+u)}{u}\) with \(u=\frac1k\to0\). Since \(\frac{\ln(1+u)}u\to1\) (l’Hôpital, or the derivative of \(\ln\) at \(1\)), \(\ln a_k\to-1\), so \(a_k\to e^{-1}\approx0.368\ne0\) by continuity of the exponential. The series diverges. Check: \(a_{100}=\left(\frac{100}{101}\right)^{100}\approx0.3697\).

items.title: Group 2: The Integral Test
items.text:
Example 10.4.18: A linear denominator

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{2k+3}\) converge?

Solution. Let \(f(x)=\dfrac1{2x+3}\): positive, continuous, and decreasing on \([1,\infty)\) because \(f'(x)=-\dfrac2{(2x+3)^2}<0\). Then \(\displaystyle\int_1^b\frac{dx}{2x+3}=\frac12\ln(2b+3)-\frac12\ln5\to\infty\). The integral diverges, so the series diverges. (It behaves like half of the harmonic series.)

Example 10.4.19: An arctangent integral, with bounds

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2+4}\) converges and trap its sum.

Solution. \(f(x)=\dfrac1{x^2+4}\) is positive and continuous, and \(f'(x)=-\dfrac{2x}{(x^2+4)^2}<0\) for \(x>0\), so it is decreasing on \([1,\infty)\). Then

\[\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2+4}=\lim_{b\to\infty}\frac12\arctan\frac b2-\frac12\arctan\frac12=\frac12\left(\frac\pi2-\arctan\frac12\right)\approx0.5536 ,\]

so the series converges. By part (b), \(0.5536<S<a_1+0.5536=\frac15+0.5536=0.7536\).

items.title: Group 3: \(p\)-series and combinations
items.text:
Example 10.4.20: Reading off \(p\)

Which of these converge? (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac3{k^{1.5}}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^{-0.8}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k\sqrt[4]{k}}\); (d) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\).

Solution. Write each as a multiple of \(k^{-p}\) and compare \(p\) with \(1\). (a) \(p=1.5>1\): converges (a constant multiple of a convergent series converges). (b) \(p=0.8\le1\): diverges. (c) \(k\sqrt[4]k=k^{5/4}\), so \(p=1.25>1\): converges. (d) \(p=\frac12\le1\): diverges.

Example 10.4.21: Combining \(p\)-series with other series

Decide (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left[\frac4{k^3}+\left(\frac23\right)^k\right]\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left[\frac7{\sqrt k}-\frac1{k^2}\right]\).

Solution. (a) \(\sum\frac4{k^3}\) converges (\(p=3\)) and \(\sum\left(\frac23\right)^k\) converges (geometric, \(|r|<1\), value \(2\)), so the sum of the two converges by property (3) of Theorem 10.3.11. (b) \(\sum\frac7{\sqrt k}\) diverges (property (2) applied to the divergent \(p\)-series with \(p=\frac12\)), while \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\) converges (\(p=2\)); by property (4) the difference diverges. Note that (b) is not an \(\infty-\infty\) problem: exactly one of the two pieces diverges.

items.title: Group 4: Hypotheses and the starting index
items.text:
Example 10.4.22: Decreasing from \(x=2\) on

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{\ln k}{k^2}\) converges.

Solution. Let \(f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}\). Then \(f'(x)=\dfrac{1-2\ln x}{x^3}\), which is negative when \(\ln x>\frac12\), that is \(x>e^{1/2}\approx1.65\). So \(f\) is positive on \((1,\infty)\) and decreasing on \([2,\infty)\), and we use \(N=2\). Integrating by parts,

\[\int_2^\infty\frac{\ln x}{x^2}\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\Big[-\frac{\ln x+1}x\Big]_2^b=\frac{\ln2+1}2\approx0.847 .\]

So \(\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{\ln k}{k^2}\) converges. The term at \(k=1\) is \(\ln1=0\) and does not matter in any case, so the original series converges.

Example 10.4.23: A longer wait for monotonicity

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty ke^{-k/3}\) converges.

Solution. Let \(f(x)=xe^{-x/3}\). Then \(f'(x)=\left(1-\dfrac x3\right)e^{-x/3}\), positive for \(x<3\) and negative for \(x>3\). So \(f\) increases up to \(x=3\) and decreases afterwards: the terms are \(a_1\approx0.72\), \(a_2\approx1.03\), \(a_3\approx1.10\), \(a_4\approx1.05,\dots\). We use \(N=3\). Then

\[\int_3^\infty xe^{-x/3}\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\Big[-(3x+9)e^{-x/3}\Big]_3^b=\frac{18}e\approx6.62 ,\]

so \(\sum_{k=3}^\infty ke^{-k/3}\) converges, hence the series from \(k=1\) converges (property (5)). The first term that is larger than its successor is \(a_3\): this is why \(N=1\) or \(N=2\) would be wrong.

items.title: Group 5: Estimates and remainders
items.text:
Example 10.4.24: Bracketing \(\sum1/k^4\)

Bracket \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^4}\) using \(n=5\).

Solution. \(s_5=1+\frac1{16}+\frac1{81}+\frac1{256}+\frac1{625}\approx1.080352\). With \(f(x)=x^{-4}\), \(\int_n^\infty f=\frac1{3n^3}\), so \(\int_6^\infty f=\frac1{648}\approx0.001543\) and \(\int_5^\infty f=\frac1{375}\approx0.002667\). Hence

\[1.081895\approx s_5+\frac1{648}<S<s_5+\frac1{375}\approx1.083019 .\]

The exact sum is \(\frac{\pi^4}{90}\approx1.082323\), inside the bracket, as the theorem promises, and the bracket is only \(0.0011\) wide after five terms.

Example 10.4.25: Terms needed for six decimal places

How many terms of \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^3}\) guarantee an error less than \(10^{-6}\)?

Solution. Use the upper bound \(R_n<\int_n^\infty x^{-3}\,dx=\frac1{2n^2}\). We need \(\frac1{2n^2}\le10^{-6}\), that is \(n^2\ge500000\), so \(n\ge\sqrt{500000}\approx707.1\) and \(n=708\) is the smallest integer that the bound guarantees. Check: \(\frac1{2\cdot708^2}\approx9.97\times10^{-7}<10^{-6}\), while \(\frac1{2\cdot707^2}\approx1.0004\times10^{-6}>10^{-6}\). Compare with the geometric series: there six decimal places needed a few dozen terms; here \(700\) terms are needed because the terms shrink only like \(\frac1{k^3}\).

items.title: Group 6: Applications: harmonic bounds and slow convergence
items.text:
Example 10.4.26: Bounding the harmonic numbers

Show that \(\ln(n+1)<H_n<1+\ln n\) for \(n\ge2\), and use this to say roughly how many terms make \(H_n\) exceed \(20\).

Solution. Apply part (c) of the Integral Test to \(f(x)=\frac1x\) with \(N=1\): \(\int_1^{n+1}\frac{dx}x<H_n<1+\int_1^n\frac{dx}x\), that is \(\ln(n+1)<H_n<1+\ln n\). For instance \(n=1000\): \(6.909<H_{1000}\approx7.485<7.908\). For \(H_n>20\) it is sufficient that \(\ln(n+1)\ge20\), i.e. \(n\ge e^{20}-1\approx4.9\times10^8\), and it is necessary that \(1+\ln n>20\), i.e. \(n>e^{19}\approx1.8\times10^8\). So about \(10^8\) to \(10^9\) terms are needed (the true value is near \(2.7\times10^8\)): a computer could do it, but no table by hand would.

Example 10.4.27: A convergent series that no table can sum

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^{1.1}}\) converges and explain why partial sums approximate it badly.

Solution. It is a \(p\)-series with \(p=1.1>1\), so it converges, and by Theorem 10.4.11 its sum lies between \(\frac1{0.1}=10\) and \(11\) (it is about \(10.58\)). The remainder satisfies \(R_n<\int_n^\infty x^{-1.1}\,dx=10\,n^{-0.1}\). After a million terms the bound is \(10\cdot(10^6)^{-0.1}=10\cdot10^{-0.6}\approx2.5\), so the first million terms may still be about \(2.5\) short of the sum (in fact \(s_{10^6}\approx8.07\)). To guarantee \(R_n<0.01\) we would need \(10\,n^{-0.1}<0.01\), that is \(n^{0.1}>1000\) and \(n>10^{30}\). Convergence is a statement about the infinite tail, and for \(p\) close to \(1\) the tail is enormous.

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 10.4.28: Using the harmonic series in a proof

Prove that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{2k}\) diverges.

Plan. Suppose it converged; use property (1) to make the harmonic series converge, which is false.

Proof. Suppose \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{2k}\) converged, to \(A\). By property (1) of Theorem 10.3.11 with \(c=2\), the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty2\cdot\frac1{2k}=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1k\) would converge (to \(2A\)). But the harmonic series diverges (Theorem 10.4.4). This contradiction shows that \(\sum\frac1{2k}\) diverges. ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to say “the terms tend to \(0\), so it converges”, which is the reverse of the Divergence Test.

Example 10.4.29: Bounds for every \(p\)-series

Prove that for \(p>1\), \(\ \dfrac1{p-1}<\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\dfrac1{k^p}<\dfrac p{p-1}\), and use it to bound \(\sum\frac1{k^{3/2}}\).

Plan. Apply part (b) of the Integral Test to \(f(x)=x^{-p}\) with \(N=1\).

Proof. For \(p>1\) the function \(f(x)=x^{-p}\) is continuous, positive and decreasing on \([1,\infty)\) (because \(f'(x)=-px^{-p-1}<0\)), and \(a_k=f(k)=k^{-p}\). The improper integral is \(\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\frac{b^{1-p}-1}{1-p}=\frac1{p-1}\), since \(b^{1-p}\to0\). By the Integral Test (b), \(I<S<a_1+I\) with \(I=\frac1{p-1}\) and \(a_1=1\), so \(\frac1{p-1}<S<1+\frac1{p-1}=\frac p{p-1}\). ◻ ∎

For \(p=\frac32\) this gives \(2<\sum\frac1{k^{3/2}}<3\) (the true value is about \(2.612\)). A common mistake is to forget that part (b) has strict inequalities and the upper bound contains the first term \(a_1\).

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 10.4.1. (a) \(a_k=\frac{3k+1}{2k+5}\to\frac32\ne0\): the series diverges. (b) \(a_k=(-1)^k\) has no limit (it alternates between \(1\) and \(-1\)), so it does not tend to \(0\): the series diverges. (c) \(\frac1{k+10}\to0\): the test is inconclusive (and in fact the series diverges, since it is the harmonic series with the first ten terms missing, by property (5) of series; but the Divergence Test cannot show that).

Knowledge Check 10.4.2. (a) \(f(x)=\frac1{3x+2}\) is positive, continuous and decreasing on \([1,\infty)\); \(\int_1^b\frac{dx}{3x+2}=\frac13\ln(3b+2)-\frac13\ln5\to\infty\), so the series diverges. (b) \(f(x)=\frac{2x}{(x^2+1)^2}\) is positive and continuous, and \(f'(x)=\frac{2(1-3x^2)}{(x^2+1)^3}<0\) for \(x\ge1\); \(\int_1^\infty f=\lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\frac1{x^2+1}\right]_1^b=\frac12\), so the series converges, and its sum is between \(\frac12\) and \(\frac12+a_1=\frac12+\frac12=1\).

Knowledge Check 10.4.3. (a) By property (1) the series converges exactly when \(\sum k^{-p}\) does, that is, when \(p>1\). (b) Theorem 10.4.11 with \(p=3\) gives \(\frac1{3-1}<S<\frac3{3-1}\), that is \(\frac12<S<\frac32\). (c) \(\frac1{\sqrt{k^3}}=k^{-3/2}\), so \(p=\frac32>1\) and it converges.

items.title: 10.5 Comparison Tests
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

The Integral Test settles \(\sum\frac1{k^2+4}\) in two lines, but try it on \(\sum\frac{5k^4-2k^2+3}{2k^6-k+5}\): the antiderivative is a nightmare, and the function is not obviously decreasing. Yet to the eye this series is just \(\sum\frac5{2k^2}\) in disguise: for large \(k\) the lower-order terms hardly matter. This section turns that impression into theorems. If the terms of a series are smaller than the terms of a series that converges, the smaller series converges too; and if the terms of two series have a positive ratio in the long run, the two series behave alike. The yardsticks are the two families we can already decide completely: geometric series and \(p\)-series.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • state and prove the Comparison Test and the Limit Comparison Test (all cases);

  • choose a comparison series from the dominant behaviour of the terms, using geometric series and \(p\)-series as yardsticks;

  • say why an inequality that points the wrong way proves nothing, and repair it;

  • explain which cases of the Limit Comparison Test are conclusive;

  • use a comparison to bound a sum and to find how many terms give a given accuracy.

Throughout, the series have terms \(\ge0\) (positive terms, in the language of the tests); the next section deals with series whose terms change sign.

items.title: The Comparison Test
items.text:
Convergence depends only on the tail of a series (Theorem 10.3.11(5)), so an inequality between terms is needed only from some index \(N\) on.

Theorem 10.5.1: Comparison Test

Let \(\sum a_k\) and \(\sum b_k\) be series and let \(N\) be an integer with \(0\le a_k\le b_k\) for all \(k\ge N\).

(1) If \(\sum b_k\) converges, then \(\sum a_k\) converges, and \(\sum_{k=N}^\infty a_k\le\sum_{k=N}^\infty b_k\).

(2) If \(\sum a_k\) diverges, then \(\sum b_k\) diverges.

(3) If \(\sum b_k\) converges, then for every \(n\ge N\) the remainders satisfy \(0\le\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty a_k\le\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty b_k\).

Proof. By Theorem 10.3.11(5) we may drop the terms before index \(N\) from both series without changing whether they converge, so assume both start at \(k=N\). Let \(s_n=\sum_{k=N}^{N+n-1}a_k\) and \(t_n=\sum_{k=N}^{N+n-1}b_k\) be the partial sums. Because \(a_k\le b_k\), adding the first \(n\) inequalities gives \(0\le s_n\le t_n\) for every \(n\).

(1) Let \(B=\sum_{k=N}^\infty b_k\). The terms of \(\sum b_k\) are \(\ge0\), so \(t_n\le B\) by Theorem 10.3.13(a). Hence \(s_n\le t_n\le B\) for all \(n\): the partial sums of \(\sum a_k\) are bounded above. The terms \(a_k\) are \(\ge0\), so by Theorem 10.3.13(a) the series converges, to a number \(A\). Finally \(s_n\le t_n\) for all \(n\) and limits preserve non-strict inequalities (Theorem C.1), so \(A\le B\).

(2) This is the contrapositive of (1): if \(\sum b_k\) converged, then \(\sum a_k\) would converge.

(3) Suppose \(\sum b_k\) converges and \(n\ge N\). The tail \(\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty b_k\) converges by Theorem 10.3.11(5), and \(0\le a_k\le b_k\) for \(k\ge n+1\). Apply (1) with \(N\) replaced by \(n+1\). ◻ ∎

Read part (2) as: if the smaller series diverges, so does the larger one. Part (1) says the same for convergence in the other direction. The two remaining combinations say nothing, and we return to that below. Because a constant factor \(c>0\) does not change convergence (Theorem 10.3.11), the test also works with \(a_k\le cb_k\) for some constant \(c>0\).

The yardsticks

Every comparison needs a series whose behaviour we already know. We have two families. The geometric series \(\sum r^k\) converges if and only if \(\abs r<1\) (Theorem 10.3.3); the \(p\)-series \(\sum\frac1{k^p}\) converges if and only if \(p>1\) (Theorem 10.4.11). Constant multiples and finitely many changed terms do not matter.

Example 10.5.2: Comparing with a geometric or a \(p\)-series

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{3^k+k}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac k{k^4+2}\) converge.

Solution. (a) Make the denominator smaller to make the fraction larger: \(3^k+k>3^k\), so \(\frac1{3^k+k}<\left(\frac13\right)^k\). The geometric series with \(r=\frac13\) converges, so \(\sum\frac1{3^k+k}\) converges by the Comparison Test, and its sum is less than \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left(\frac13\right)^k=\frac{1/3}{1-1/3}=\frac12\). (Its value is about \(0.392\).) (b) Here \(k^4+2>k^4\), so \(\frac k{k^4+2}<\frac k{k^4}=\frac1{k^3}\). The \(p\)-series with \(p=3\) converges, so the series converges.

Example 10.5.3: Comparison for divergence

Show that (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt k-1}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=3}^\infty\frac{\ln k}k\) diverge.

Solution. Now the comparison series must be the smaller one, and it must diverge. (a) For \(k\ge2\), \(0<\sqrt k-1<\sqrt k\), so \(\frac1{\sqrt k-1}>\frac1{\sqrt k}\). Since \(\sum\frac1{\sqrt k}\) is a \(p\)-series with \(p=\frac12\le1\), it diverges, and so does the larger series. (b) For \(k\ge3\) we have \(\ln k\ge\ln3\approx1.0986>1\), so \(\frac{\ln k}k>\frac1k\). The harmonic series diverges, so \(\sum_{k=3}^\infty\frac{\ln k}k\) diverges. (The inequality fails at \(k=2\), since \(\ln2\approx0.693<1\); the Comparison Test only needs it from some \(N\) on.)

What each inequality can and cannot say

Let \(0\le a_k\le b_k\). If \(\sum b_k\) converges, so does \(\sum a_k\). If \(\sum a_k\) diverges, so does \(\sum b_k\). But if \(\sum b_k\) diverges, or if \(\sum a_k\) converges, the Comparison Test gives no conclusion: a series can be smaller than a divergent one and still converge (\(\frac1{k^2}\le\frac1k\)) or diverge (\(\frac1{2k}\le\frac1k\)). In short, a convergent series can only be used as an upper bound and a divergent series only as a lower bound.

Example 10.5.4: An inequality that points the wrong way

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k^2-1}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k+1}\) converge.

Solution. (a) The tempting comparison is with \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\), which converges. But \(k^2-1<k^2\) gives \(\frac1{k^2-1}>\frac1{k^2}\): our series is larger than a convergent one, and that says nothing. Repair: we need a convergent series that is larger. For \(k\ge2\), \(k^2-1\ge\frac{k^2}2\) (this is \(k^2\ge2\)), so \(\frac1{k^2-1}\le\frac2{k^2}\), and \(\sum\frac2{k^2}\) converges. So the series converges. (In fact it telescopes, \(\frac1{k^2-1}=\frac12\left(\frac1{k-1}-\frac1{k+1}\right)\), with sum \(\frac34\), so the comparison led to the right answer.) (b) Compare with \(\sum\frac1k\), which diverges: \(\frac1{k+1}<\frac1k\) is a smaller series than a divergent one, so again nothing follows. Repair: \(k+1\le2k\) for \(k\ge1\), so \(\frac1{k+1}\ge\frac1{2k}\), and \(\sum\frac1{2k}\) diverges (Theorem 10.3.11(2)). So the series diverges.

Knowledge Check 10.5.1: Choosing a comparison

For each series, name a comparison series and say whether the inequality should make the given series smaller or larger than it: (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{4^k+k}\); (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2+9}\); (c) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k-1}\).

Pause and think 10.5.1: Why nonnegative terms?

Let \(a_k=-1\) and \(b_k=\frac1{k^2}\). Then \(a_k\le b_k\) for every \(k\) and \(\sum b_k\) converges. Does \(\sum a_k\) converge? Which line of the proof of the Comparison Test fails?

Answer and discussion

\(\sum a_k=-1-1-1-\cdots\) diverges (to \(-\infty\)). The proof breaks at the first claim: “\(s_n\le t_n\le B\) gives bounded above, so converges” relies on the partial sums being nondecreasing, which needs \(a_k\ge0\). Here the partial sums decrease without bound; being bounded above does not help. Nonnegativity is what turns “bounded above” into “convergent”.

items.title: The Limit Comparison Test
items.text:
Inequalities can be fiddly. The series \(\sum rac1{3^k-k}\) lies above \(\sum3^{-k}\), so the easy comparison goes the wrong way, even though the two series plainly behave alike. The Limit Comparison Test compares the terms by their ratio.

Theorem 10.5.5: Limit Comparison Test

Let \(a_k>0\) and \(b_k>0\) for all \(k\) from some index on, and let \(L=\displaystyle\lim_{k o\infty} rac{a_k}{b_k}\).

(1) If \(0<L<\infty\), then \(\sum a_k\) and \(\sum b_k\) either both converge or both diverge.

(2) If \(L=0\) and \(\sum b_k\) converges, then \(\sum a_k\) converges.

(3) If \(L=\infty\) and \(\sum b_k\) diverges, then \(\sum a_k\) diverges.

Proof. (1) Take \(\varepsilon= rac L2>0\) in the definition of the limit: there is \(K\) such that \(\abs{ rac{a_k}{b_k}-L}< rac L2\) for \(k>K\), that is, \( rac L2< rac{a_k}{b_k}< rac{3L}2\). Multiplying by \(b_k>0\),

\[ rac L2\,b_k<a_k< rac{3L}2\,b_k\qquad(k>K).\]

If \(\sum b_k\) converges, then \(\sum rac{3L}2b_k\) converges (Theorem 10.3.11(1)), and \(0<a_k< rac{3L}2b_k\), so \(\sum a_k\) converges by the Comparison Test (1). If \(\sum b_k\) diverges, then \(\sum rac L2b_k\) diverges (Theorem 10.3.11(2), since \( rac L2 e0\)), and \(0< rac L2b_k<a_k\), so \(\sum a_k\) diverges by the Comparison Test (2). So \(\sum b_k\) converges \(\Rightarrow\) \(\sum a_k\) converges, and \(\sum b_k\) diverges \(\Rightarrow\) \(\sum a_k\) diverges; the second statement is equivalent to “\(\sum a_k\) converges \(\Rightarrow\) \(\sum b_k\) converges”, so the two series converge or diverge together.

(2) Take \(\varepsilon=1\): there is \(K\) with \(0< rac{a_k}{b_k}<1\), so \(0<a_k<b_k\) for \(k>K\). If \(\sum b_k\) converges, so does \(\sum a_k\), by the Comparison Test (1).

(3) \(L=\infty\) means that for every number \(M\) there is \(K\) with \( rac{a_k}{b_k}>M\) for \(k>K\). Take \(M=1\): \(a_k>b_k>0\) for \(k>K\). If \(\sum b_k\) diverges, the larger series \(\sum a_k\) diverges by the Comparison Test (2). ◻ ∎

Cases (2) and (3) are one-sided: they are conclusive only when the comparison series behaves in the stated way. If \(L=0\) and \(\sum b_k\) diverges, or \(L=\infty\) and \(\sum b_k\) converges, the test says nothing (Example 10.5.9).

Procedure 10.5.6: Choosing a comparison series

  1. Check the Divergence Test first: if \(a_k ot o0\), the series diverges and no comparison is needed.

  2. Find what \(a_k\) is like for large \(k\): keep the highest power in a rational expression, the largest exponential, and discard the rest.

  3. Take \(b_k\) to be that simplified term without its constant factor: a \(p\)-series or a geometric series.

  4. Try the Comparison Test if the inequality is easy and points the right way (smaller than a convergent series, or larger than a divergent one); otherwise compute \(L=\lim rac{a_k}{b_k}\).

  5. If \(L\) is \(0\) or \(\infty\), check that it is a conclusive case; if not, change \(b_k\).

Example 10.5.7: Rational terms

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{k+3}{k^3-k+2}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{4k^2-k}{k^3+7}\) converge.

Solution. (a) The terms are positive, and for large \(k\) they behave like \( rac k{k^3}= rac1{k^2}\). Take \(b_k= rac1{k^2}\) (convergent). Then

\[L=\lim_{k o\infty} rac{k^2(k+3)}{k^3-k+2}=\lim_{k o\infty} rac{1+3/k}{1-1/k^2+2/k^3}=1 .\]

Since \(0<L<\infty\), the series converges.

(b) The terms behave like \( rac{4k^2}{k^3}= rac4k\). Take \(b_k= rac1k\) (divergent). Then \(L=\lim rac{k(4k^2-k)}{k^3+7}=\lim rac{4-1/k}{1+7/k^3}=4\), so the series diverges.

Example 10.5.8: Roots in the terms

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{\sqrt{k+1}}{k^2+3}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{3\sqrt k+2}{k+5}\) converge.

Solution. (a) For large \(k\), \( rac{\sqrt{k+1}}{k^2+3}\approx rac{k^{1/2}}{k^2}= rac1{k^{3/2}}\), a convergent \(p\)-series (\(p= rac32\)). Then \(L=\lim rac{k^{3/2}\sqrt{k+1}}{k^2+3}=\lim rac{k^2\sqrt{1+1/k}}{k^2+3}=1\), so the series converges. (b) The terms behave like \( rac{3\sqrt k}k= rac3{\sqrt k}\). Take \(b_k= rac1{\sqrt k}\) (divergent, \(p= rac12\)): \(L=\lim rac{\sqrt k\,(3\sqrt k+2)}{k+5}=\lim rac{3k+2\sqrt k}{k+5}=3\), so the series diverges.

Example 10.5.9: A logarithm between two \(p\)-series

Decide whether \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty rac{\ln k}{k^{3/2}}\) converges.

Solution. Since \(\ln k\) grows, the terms are a little larger than \( rac1{k^{3/2}}\) and much smaller than \( rac1k\). Try both: with \(b_k= rac1{k^{3/2}}\) (convergent), \(L=\lim\ln k=\infty\), which is the inconclusive case; with \(b_k= rac1k\) (divergent), \(L=\lim rac{\ln k}{\sqrt k}=0\), again inconclusive. So choose a \(p\)-series between them, \(b_k= rac1{k^{5/4}}\) (convergent, \(p= rac54>1\)):

\[L=\lim_{k o\infty} rac{\ln k/k^{3/2}}{1/k^{5/4}}=\lim_{k o\infty} rac{\ln k}{k^{1/4}}=0 ,\]

by l’Hôpital’s Rule (the quotient of derivatives is \( rac4{k^{1/4}} o0\)). This is a conclusive case, so the series converges.

Example 10.5.10: Exponentials, and checking the Divergence Test first

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{2^k+k}{3^k-1}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{3\cdot2^k-1}{2^k+7}\) converge.

Solution. (a) The dominant terms give \( rac{2^k}{3^k}\), so take \(b_k=\left( rac23 ight)^k\), a convergent geometric series. Then \(L=\lim rac{(2^k+k)\,3^k}{(3^k-1)\,2^k}=\lim rac{1+k/2^k}{1-3^{-k}}=1\) (because \( rac k{2^k} o0\)). The series converges. (b) No comparison is needed: \(a_k= rac{3-2^{-k}}{1+7\cdot2^{-k}} o3 e0\), so the series diverges by the Divergence Test. Comparing first would have wasted effort.

Knowledge Check 10.5.2: The Limit Comparison Test

In each case \(a_k,b_k>0\). Say whether the Limit Comparison Test is conclusive, and what it concludes. (a) \(a_k= rac1{k^2}\), \(b_k= rac1{k^{3/2}}\). (b) \(a_k= rac1k\), \(b_k= rac1{k^2}\). (c) \(a_k= rac{2k+1}{k^2}\), \(b_k= rac1k\).

Pause and think 10.5.2: Both sides of the ratio

Find two series \(\sum a_k\) with \(\lim rac{a_k}{1/k}=0\), one convergent and one divergent. (Use Theorem 10.4.11 and the series of Example 10.4.9.) What does this say about the case \(L=0\) with a divergent comparison series?

Answer and discussion

\(a_k= rac1{k^2}\): \( rac{a_k}{1/k}= rac1k o0\) and \(\sum a_k\) converges. \(a_k= rac1{k\ln k}\) (from \(k=2\)): \( rac{a_k}{1/k}= rac1{\ln k} o0\) and \(\sum a_k\) diverges (Example 10.4.9). So \(L=0\) with a divergent \(\sum b_k\) can go either way: the test is inconclusive.

Example 10.5.11: Bounded oscillation in the numerator

Decide whether (a) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{2+\sin k}{k^2+1}\) and (b) \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty rac{2+\cos k}{\sqrt k}\) converge.

Solution. The numerators oscillate but stay between \(1\) and \(3\), since \(-1\le\sin k,\cos k\le1\); so all terms are positive. (a) \( rac{2+\sin k}{k^2+1}\le rac3{k^2+1}< rac3{k^2}\), and \(\sum rac3{k^2}\) converges: the series converges. (b) \( rac{2+\cos k}{\sqrt k}\ge rac1{\sqrt k}\), and \(\sum rac1{\sqrt k}\) diverges (\(p= rac12\)): the series diverges. The limit \(\lim rac{2+\sin k}{k^2+1}\cdot k^2\) does not exist, so the Limit Comparison Test would not help here; the Comparison Test does.

items.title: Estimating a sum by comparison
items.text:
Part (3) of the Comparison Test turns a comparison into a numerical method: a series that is smaller than a series we can sum or bound has a sum that is smaller, and so does every remainder.

Example 10.5.12: Bounds for a sum, and a remainder

Let \(S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{2^k+k}\). (a) Trap \(S\) between two simple numbers. (b) Use \(s_4=\sum_{k=1}^4\frac1{2^k+k}\) and a remainder bound to find a shorter interval.

Solution. (a) Since \(k<2^k\), \(2^k<2^k+k<2\cdot2^k\), so \(\frac1{2}\cdot2^{-k}<a_k<2^{-k}\). Sum from \(k=1\): \(\sum2^{-k}=1\) and \(\sum\frac12\cdot2^{-k}=\frac12\), so by the Comparison Test (1) \(\frac12\le S\le1\). (In fact \(S\approx0.697\).) (b) The first four terms are \(\frac13,\frac16,\frac1{11},\frac1{20}\), so \(s_4=\frac{141}{220}\approx0.6409\). For the remainder use part (3) with \(b_k=2^{-k}\): \(0\le R_4=\sum_{k=5}^\infty a_k\le\sum_{k=5}^\infty2^{-k}=\frac1{16}\). Therefore \(0.6409<S<0.6409+0.0625=0.7034\). The interval is about \(0.06\) wide and contains \(0.697\).

Knowledge Check 10.5.3: Estimating by comparison

Let \(S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{4^k+1}\). Use the Comparison Test twice to show that \(\frac16\le S<\frac13\).

Pause and think 10.5.3: Does comparison give the value?

If \(0<a_k<b_k\) for every \(k\) and both series converge, must \(\sum a_k<\sum b_k\) strictly, or could the sums be equal? (Look at the series \(\sum(b_k-a_k)\).)

Answer and discussion

The sums cannot be equal. The series \(\sum(b_k-a_k)\) has positive terms and converges (Theorem 10.3.11(3)) to \(\sum b_k-\sum a_k\). A convergent series of positive terms has a value at least its first term (Theorem 10.3.13), so \(\sum b_k-\sum a_k\ge b_1-a_1>0\). The comparison gives bounds, never the value.

Example 10.5.13: A power of a logarithm

Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{(\ln k)^k}\) converges.

Solution. The terms start large (\(a_2\approx2.08\)) but fall quickly. Since \(e^2\approx7.39<8\), for \(k\ge8\) we have \(\ln k\ge\ln8\approx2.079>2\), so \((\ln k)^k>2^k\) and \(\frac1{(\ln k)^k}<\left(\frac12\right)^k\). The geometric series with \(r=\frac12\) converges, so by the Comparison Test (with \(N=8\)) the series converges. The first six terms do not matter for convergence.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Fourteen further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Direct comparison with a geometric or a \(p\)-series (Examples 10.5.14–10.5.15).

  2. Inequalities that point the wrong way, and repairs (Examples 10.5.16–10.5.17).

  3. The Limit Comparison Test (Examples 10.5.18–10.5.19).

  4. Logarithms (Examples 10.5.20–10.5.21).

  5. Estimating sums by comparison (Examples 10.5.22–10.5.23).

  6. Applications: a parameter and a trigonometric term (Examples 10.5.24–10.5.25).

  7. Proofs (Examples 10.5.26–10.5.27).

items.title: Group 1: Direct comparison
items.text:
Example 10.5.14: A geometric upper bound

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac3{2^k+k^2}\) converge?

Solution. Since \(k^2>0\), \(2^k+k^2>2^k\), so \(\frac3{2^k+k^2}<\frac3{2^k}=3\left(\frac12\right)^k\). The series \(\sum3\left(\frac12\right)^k\) is a convergent geometric series (\(r=\frac12\)) times \(3\), so the given series converges by the Comparison Test. Check: the first terms are \(\frac34,\frac37,\frac3{17},\dots\), each smaller than \(\frac3{2^k}=\frac32,\frac34,\frac38,\dots\)

Example 10.5.15: Bounding the numerator as well

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{k+1}{k^3+2}\) converge?

Solution. Make the fraction larger in two steps: the numerator satisfies \(k+1\le2k\) for \(k\ge1\), and the denominator \(k^3+2>k^3\). Hence \(\frac{k+1}{k^3+2}\le\frac{2k}{k^3}=\frac2{k^2}\). The \(p\)-series with \(p=2\) converges, so the series converges. Check at \(k=1\): \(\frac23\le2\); at \(k=10\): \(\frac{11}{1002}\approx0.011\le0.02\).

items.title: Group 2: Wrong-way inequalities
items.text:
Example 10.5.16: Repairing a convergence comparison

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2-3k+3}\) converge?

Solution. The denominator is positive for all \(k\) (its discriminant is \(9-12<0\)). For \(k\ge2\), \(k^2-3k+3<k^2\), so the terms are larger than \(\frac1{k^2}\): no conclusion from that. We need a lower bound for the denominator of the form \(ck^2\). Completing the square, \(k^2-3k+3=\frac{k^2}4+\frac34(k-2)^2\ge\frac{k^2}4\), so \(\frac1{k^2-3k+3}\le\frac4{k^2}\) for every \(k\ge1\). The series \(\sum\frac4{k^2}\) converges, so the given series converges.

Example 10.5.17: Repairing a divergence comparison

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt k+3}\) converge?

Solution. Comparing with \(\frac1{\sqrt k}\) gives \(\frac1{\sqrt k+3}<\frac1{\sqrt k}\): the given series is smaller than a divergent one, which proves nothing. Instead find a divergent series below it: for \(k\ge1\), \(3\le3\sqrt k\), so \(\sqrt k+3\le4\sqrt k\) and \(\frac1{\sqrt k+3}\ge\frac1{4\sqrt k}\). Since \(\sum\frac1{4\sqrt k}\) diverges (\(p=\frac12\), constant factor \(\frac14\)), the series diverges.

items.title: Group 3: The Limit Comparison Test
items.text:
Example 10.5.18: A rational function with a quartic denominator

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{2k^2+5}{k^4-3k+9}\) converge?

Solution. The denominator is positive (\(k^4-3k+9=7,19,81,253,\dots\) for \(k=1,2,3,4\) and increasing), so the terms are positive. They behave like \(\frac{2k^2}{k^4}=\frac2{k^2}\); take \(b_k=\frac1{k^2}\). Then \(L=\lim\frac{k^2(2k^2+5)}{k^4-3k+9}=\lim\frac{2+5/k^2}{1-3/k^3+9/k^4}=2\). Since \(0<L<\infty\) and \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\) converges, the series converges.

Example 10.5.19: A square root in the denominator

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac k{\sqrt{k^5+3}}\) converge?

Solution. For large \(k\), \(\sqrt{k^5+3}\approx k^{5/2}\), so the terms behave like \(\frac k{k^{5/2}}=\frac1{k^{3/2}}\). With \(b_k=\frac1{k^{3/2}}\) (convergent),

\[L=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{k\cdot k^{3/2}}{\sqrt{k^5+3}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{k^{5/2}}{\sqrt{k^5+3}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac1{\sqrt{1+3/k^5}}=1 .\]

Since \(0<L<\infty\), the series converges.

items.title: Group 4: Logarithms
items.text:
Example 10.5.20: One over the logarithm

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{\ln k}\) converge?

Solution. The terms tend to \(0\), but slowly. Since \(\ln k<k\) for every \(k\ge2\) (the function \(x-\ln x\) has derivative \(1-\frac1x>0\) for \(x>1\) and equals \(1>0\) at \(x=1\)), we get \(\frac1{\ln k}>\frac1k\). The harmonic series diverges, so the larger series diverges.

Example 10.5.21: A squared logarithm

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{(\ln k)^2}{k^3}\) converge?

Solution. Try \(b_k=\frac1{k^3}\) (convergent): \(L=\lim(\ln k)^2=\infty\), inconclusive. Take the larger \(p\)-series \(b_k=\frac1{k^{5/2}}\) (convergent, \(p=\frac52>1\)): \(L=\lim\frac{(\ln k)^2}{k^{1/2}}\). Apply l’Hôpital’s Rule twice: \(\frac{2\ln x/x}{\frac12x^{-1/2}}=\frac{4\ln x}{x^{1/2}}\), and then \(\frac{4/x}{\frac12x^{-1/2}}=\frac8{x^{1/2}}\to0\). So \(L=0\) with a convergent \(\sum b_k\), which is conclusive: the series converges.

items.title: Group 5: Estimating sums by comparison
items.text:
Example 10.5.22: Two-sided bounds for a \(p\)-series relative

Let \(S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2+3}\). Bound \(S\), then sharpen the bound with ten terms.

Solution. For \(k\ge1\), \(k^2<k^2+3\le4k^2\), so \(\frac1{4k^2}\le\frac1{k^2+3}<\frac1{k^2}\). Using \(\sum\frac1{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}6\approx1.645\) (the value stated in Section 10.3), \(\frac{\pi^2}{24}\le S<\frac{\pi^2}6\), that is \(0.411\le S<1.645\). To sharpen, take \(s_{10}=\sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac1{k^2+3}\approx0.6459\) and bound the tail by comparison with \(\sum_{k>10}\frac1{k^2}<\int_{10}^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2}=\frac1{10}\) (Theorem 10.4.13): \(0.6459<S<0.7459\). The true value is \(\approx0.7403\), near the top, because the terms \(\frac1{k^2+3}\) are close to \(\frac1{k^2}\) for large \(k\).

Example 10.5.23: Accuracy \(10^{-4}\) from a geometric tail

How many terms of \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{3^k+k}\) guarantee an error less than \(10^{-4}\), and what is the resulting estimate?

Solution. Since \(\frac1{3^k+k}<3^{-k}\), part (3) of the Comparison Test gives \(0<R_n<\sum_{k>n}3^{-k}=\frac{3^{-n}}2\) (geometric series with first term \(3^{-(n+1)}\) and \(r=\frac13\)). We need \(\frac{3^{-n}}2<10^{-4}\), i.e. \(3^n>5000\). Now \(3^7=2187<5000<6561=3^8\), so \(n=8\) terms are enough; with \(n=7\) the bound is \(\frac1{2\cdot2187}\approx2.3\times10^{-4}\), too large to guarantee anything. With \(n=8\): \(s_8\approx0.392008\) and the error is in \((0,7.7\times10^{-5})\), so \(S\approx0.39201\) to four decimals (the true value is \(0.392084\)).

items.title: Group 6: Applications
items.text:
Example 10.5.24: A parameter

For which \(p>0\) does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^p+k}\) converge?

Solution. The dominant term of the denominator depends on \(p\). If \(p>1\), \(k^p\) dominates: compare with \(b_k=\frac1{k^p}\): \(\frac{a_k}{b_k}=\frac{k^p}{k^p+k}=\frac1{1+k^{1-p}}\to1\) because \(1-p<0\). By the Limit Comparison Test the series behaves like the \(p\)-series: it converges. If \(0<p\le1\), \(k\) dominates (for \(p=1\) the denominator is exactly \(2k\)): compare with \(b_k=\frac1k\): \(\frac{a_k}{b_k}=\frac1{1+k^{p-1}}\to1\) if \(p<1\) (as \(p-1<0\)) and equals \(\frac12\) if \(p=1\). Either way \(0<L<\infty\) and the harmonic series diverges, so the series diverges. Answer: it converges if and only if \(p>1\).

Example 10.5.25: A trigonometric term

Does \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left(1-\cos\frac1k\right)\) converge?

Solution. All terms are positive (\(\cos\frac1k<1\)), and they tend to \(0\), so the Divergence Test is silent. For large \(k\), \(\frac1k\) is small and \(1-\cos u\approx\frac{u^2}2\), which suggests \(b_k=\frac1{k^2}\). With \(u=\frac1k\to0^+\),

\[L=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1-\cos(1/k)}{1/k^2}=\lim_{u\to0^+}\frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}=\lim_{u\to0^+}\frac{\sin u}{2u}=\frac12 ,\]

by l’Hôpital’s Rule and the basic limit \(\frac{\sin u}u\to1\). As \(0<L<\infty\) and \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\) converges, the series converges. Check at \(k=10\): \(1-\cos0.1\approx0.0049958\) versus \(\frac1{2\cdot100}=0.005\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 10.5.26: Geometric mean of two convergent series

Let \(a_k>0\), \(b_k>0\) and suppose \(\sum a_k\) and \(\sum b_k\) both converge. Prove that \(\sum\sqrt{a_kb_k}\) converges.

Plan. Bound \(\sqrt{a_kb_k}\) above by something whose series we know converges.

Proof. For positive numbers \(x,y\) we have \((\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2\ge0\), so \(x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\), that is \(\sqrt{xy}\le\frac{x+y}2\). With \(x=a_k\) and \(y=b_k\), \(0<\sqrt{a_kb_k}\le\frac12(a_k+b_k)\). The series \(\sum\frac12(a_k+b_k)\) converges by Theorem 10.3.11(1) and (3). By the Comparison Test, \(\sum\sqrt{a_kb_k}\) converges. ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to run the argument backwards: \(\sum\sqrt{a_kb_k}\) can converge while \(\sum a_k\) diverges (take \(a_k=1\) and \(b_k=\frac1{k^4}\), so \(\sqrt{a_kb_k}=\frac1{k^2}\)).

Example 10.5.27: A series and its “compressed” version

Let \(a_k>0\) and \(c_k=\dfrac{a_k}{1+a_k}\). Prove that \(\sum a_k\) converges if and only if \(\sum c_k\) converges.

Plan. One direction is a direct comparison. For the other, show first that \(a_k\to0\), so that \(c_k\) and \(a_k\) are nearly equal.

Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Since \(1+a_k>1\), \(0<c_k<a_k\). If \(\sum a_k\) converges, so does \(\sum c_k\) by the Comparison Test.

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(\sum c_k\) converges. Then \(c_k\to0\) (Divergence Test), so there is \(K\) with \(c_k<\frac12\) for \(k\ge K\). Solving \(c_k=\frac{a_k}{1+a_k}\) for \(a_k\) gives \(a_k=\frac{c_k}{1-c_k}\) (note \(0<c_k<1\)). For \(k\ge K\) we have \(1-c_k>\frac12\), so \(a_k<2c_k\). The series \(\sum2c_k\) converges (Theorem 10.3.11(1)), so \(\sum a_k\) converges by the Comparison Test. ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to skip showing that \(a_k\to0\): without it, \(c_k\approx a_k\) fails (if \(a_k\) is large, \(c_k\approx1\) and no comparison with \(a_k\) is possible).

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 10.5.1. (a) Compare with the geometric series \(\sum\left(\frac14\right)^k\): \(4^k+k>4^k\), so the given series is smaller than a convergent series, and converges. (b) Compare with \(\sum\frac1{k^2}\): \(k^2+9>k^2\), smaller than a convergent series, so it converges. (c) Compare with the harmonic series: \(k-1<k\) gives \(\frac1{k-1}>\frac1k\), larger than a divergent series, so \(\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac1{k-1}\) diverges (indeed it is the harmonic series shifted by one).

Knowledge Check 10.5.2. (a) \(\frac{a_k}{b_k}=\frac{k^{3/2}}{k^2}=k^{-1/2}\to0\) and \(\sum b_k\) converges (\(p=\frac32\)): conclusive, \(\sum a_k\) converges (it is also a convergent \(p\)-series). (b) \(\frac{a_k}{b_k}=k\to\infty\), but \(\sum b_k\) converges: inconclusive (and indeed \(\sum\frac1k\) diverges). (c) \(\frac{a_k}{b_k}=\frac{2k+1}k\to2\in(0,\infty)\): conclusive, both series diverge.

Knowledge Check 10.5.3. Since \(4^k<4^k+1\le2\cdot4^k\), we get \(\frac12\cdot4^{-k}\le\frac1{4^k+1}<4^{-k}\). The geometric series give \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty4^{-k}=\frac{1/4}{1-1/4}=\frac13\) and \(\sum\frac12\cdot4^{-k}=\frac16\), so by the Comparison Test (1) \(\frac16\le S\le\frac13\), and the upper inequality is strict because \(a_1=\frac15<\frac14=b_1\) (Pause and think 10.5.3). The true value is \(S\approx0.2794\).

items.title: 10.6 Alternating Series
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

The harmonic series \(1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots\) diverges. Change every second sign and you get \(1-\frac12+\frac13-\frac14+\cdots\), whose partial sums \(1,\ \frac12,\ \frac56,\ \frac7{12},\dots\) hop back and forth and seem to settle near \(0.69\). The tests of the last two sections need nonnegative terms, so none of them applies. This section handles the simplest and most important sign pattern: terms that strictly alternate. The test is short, the error is easy to control (it is smaller than the first term you leave out), and the result raises a new question: when does a series converge because of its signs, and when would it converge anyway? The answer leads to absolute and conditional convergence, which are the vocabulary of the next chapter.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • apply the Alternating Series Test, checking both conditions, and recognise when it fails or does not apply;

  • bound the error of a partial sum of an alternating series and find how many terms give a required accuracy;

  • define absolute and conditional convergence and classify a series;

  • decide convergence of every alternating \(p\)-series;

  • prove the main theorems of this section, and say why the order of terms matters for some series.

items.title: Alternating series and the Alternating Series Test
items.text:
Definition 10.6.1: Alternating series

An alternating series is a series whose terms alternate in sign, that is, a series of the form \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty(-1)^{k+1}a_k\) or \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty(-1)^ka_k\) with all \(a_k>0\) (or all \(a_k\ge0\)).

The partial sums of \(\sum\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}k\) are \(s_1=1\), \(s_2=\frac12\), \(s_3=\frac56\), \(s_4=\frac7{12}\), \(s_5=\frac{47}{60}\), \(s_6=\frac{37}{60}\). Odd partial sums lie above and even partial sums below, and each new pair closes in on the value.

This is the pattern the proof makes precise: the even partial sums increase, the odd ones decrease, and the sum is trapped between them.

Theorem 10.6.2: Alternating Series Test

Let \(a_1\ge a_2\ge a_3\ge\cdots\) and \(\lim_{k\to\infty}a_k=0\). Then \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty(-1)^{k+1}a_k\) converges. Moreover, if \(s_n\) is the \(n\)th partial sum and \(S\) the sum, then
